plan.curriculum: Mathematics 2.0, Measurement, Year 5 (VC2M5M04): measure angles in degrees with a protractor and relate the measures to angle names
plan.shape: example-first: reading a two-scale protractor is new for many, so the teacher models on both scales before any guided measuring
plan.criticalFeature: read the scale that starts at 0 on the arm you lined up
decisionPoints: the choice check on angle names
the hinge: measure with the right scale
plan.anchor: quarter turn 90°, half turn 180°, full turn 360°

manipulatives: A protractor and a ruler for every student
A large demonstration protractor, or the on-screen protractor
studentTools: Printed Worksheet for every student; Extension and Supported Worksheet as needed
routineIcons: Write it, chin it, show me
boardSetup: The anchor on the board: quarter turn 90°, half turn 180°, full turn 360°

resources.label: Worksheet
resources.description: Your turn. Name, measure, worded problems and thinking questions.
resources.title: Measuring and Classifying Angles
resources.subtitle: You need a protractor and a ruler.

steps: Compare it with a square corner (90°).
It is smaller than a square corner.
Smaller than 90° is acute.

sections.title: Measure it
sections.intro: Measure each angle with your protractor. If an arm is too short, extend it with your ruler.

steps: Put the centre on the vertex.
Line up 0 with one arm.
Count up from that 0 to the other arm.

example.prompt: A goalkeeper's arms make an angle of 110°. Name the angle.
steps: 110° is more than 90°.
110° is less than 180°.
Between 90° and 180° is obtuse.

items.prompt: A netball player stretches to catch. Her arms make an angle of 135°. Is this angle acute, obtuse or reflex? How do you know?
A skate ramp rises at 25° from the ground. Name the angle. Is it more or less than half a right angle?
items.answer: acute; less, because half a right angle is 45°

items.prompt: What angle do the hands of a clock make at 3 o'clock? What is its name?
What angle do the hands of a clock make at 6 o'clock? What is its name?
A classroom door opens 100° from closed. Name the angle.

example.prompt: Is an angle of 95° acute? Explain.
steps: Acute means less than 90°.
95° is more than 90°.
So it is not acute. It is obtuse.

items.prompt: Sam measured this angle as 130°. Is he right? Explain his mistake.
items.answer: No. It is 50°. He read the scale that starts at 0 on the other side (180° - 50° = 130°).

items.prompt: Pip says every angle bigger than 90° is obtuse. Give an angle that proves Pip wrong, and name it.
items.answer: Any angle of 180° or more, e.g. 200° is reflex, 180° is straight.

items.prompt: Draw an angle that is acute but more than half a right angle. Measure it and write its size.

resources.label: Extension
resources.description: Early finisher option. Clock-hand angles and angle puzzles, with worked examples.
resources.title: Extension: Angle Detectives
resources.subtitle: Use what you know about turns and angle names.

sections.title: Clock angles
sections.intro: A full turn is 360°. A clock has 12 numbers, so the hands turn 30° from one number to the next (360° divided by 12).

example.prompt: What angle do the hands make at 2 o'clock?
steps: Count the gaps from 12 to 2: 2 gaps.
Each gap is 30°.
2 x 30° = 60°. That is acute.

items.prompt: 10 o'clock (the smaller angle): angle and name?
8 o'clock (the smaller angle): angle and name?
At what two times on the hour is the angle 90°?

example.prompt: I am a multiple of 20. I am obtuse. I am less than 130°. What could I be?
steps: Obtuse means more than 90° and less than 180°.
Less than 130° as well.
Multiples of 20 in that range: 100 and 120.

items.prompt: I am a multiple of 25. I am obtuse. What could I be? List all the answers.
I am half of a straight angle. What am I, and what is my name?
I am a reflex angle and a multiple of 100. What am I?

example.prompt: A shot leaves at 40°. The coach says make it 15° bigger. New angle and name?
steps: Add the change: 40° + 15° = 55°.
55° is less than 90°.
So it is acute.

items.prompt: A basketball shot leaves the hand at 52°. The coach says make it 8° bigger. What is the new angle? Name it.
A footy kick leaves the boot at 35°. A player turns it a quarter turn more. What is the new angle? Name it.
A gymnast's legs start together (0°) and open to a straight line. How many degrees did they open? Name the final angle.

resources.label: Supported Worksheet
resources.description: For students who need more guidance: protractors printed on, hints on every question.
resources.title: Measuring Angles: Step by Step
resources.subtitle: Take it one step at a time.

sections.title: Smaller or bigger than a square corner?

steps: Hold the corner of your book on the angle.
The angle is smaller than the corner.
Smaller is acute.

items.hint: Smaller than the book corner? Then it is acute.
Bigger than the book corner but not a straight line? Obtuse.
Almost a straight line, but not quite.

steps: Find the 0 where the arm lies flat.
Follow that row of numbers up.
Stop where the other arm crosses: 30.

items.hint: The arm lies on the right, so start at the 0 on the right.
It is obtuse, so the answer must be over 90.
The arm lies on the left, so start at the 0 on the left.
Start at the 0 on the left and count up.

example.prompt: An angle of exactly 90° is called a ________ angle.
steps: Look at the word bank: acute, right, obtuse, straight, reflex.
Exactly 90° is a square corner.
A square corner is a right angle.

items.prompt: An angle less than 90° is called ________.
items.hint: Word bank: acute, right, obtuse, straight, reflex.

items.prompt: An angle of exactly 180° is called a ________ angle.
items.hint: It looks like a straight line.

items.prompt: An angle between 180° and 360° is called ________.
items.hint: It is bigger than a straight line.

slides.notes: Open Session 1 of the angles week. One line: today we measure angles and name them by their size.
Prep slide. Protractor and ruler for every student, boards and markers ready. Print the Worksheet for all, and a few copies of the Extension and the Supported Worksheet.

slides.title: Fraction, decimal, percentage
prompts: Write 3/4 as a decimal and as a percentage.

beats: SAY: Let's warm up with fractions, decimals and percentages from last term.
ASK: Write three quarters as a decimal and as a percentage.
20 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: 0.75 and 75%
SCAN boards, back row first.
80%+ -> reveal, move on.
Less -> shade the strip: each quarter is 25%, count them, re-ask.
REVEAL after boards are scanned.
SAY: Three quarters is 0.75, or 75%. Tick or fix.
trap: writing 0.34 for three quarters.
Fix: count the quarters as 25% each, student rewrites.
notes.prep: Daily Review from Term 3 Week 9. Whole block under 6 minutes.

beats: ASK: What is 25% of 60?
15 sec. Cue: boards up on cue.
EXPECT: 15
SCAN boards.
80%+ -> reveal, move on.
Less -> 25% is one quarter: halve 60, then halve again, re-ask.
REVEAL after boards are scanned.
SAY: Fifteen. A quarter of 60 is 15. Tick or fix.
trap: writing 25 or 35.
Fix: say 25% is one quarter, student halves twice.
notes.prep: Term 3 Week 9 retrieval: percentage of an amount.

beats: ASK: Order these from smallest to largest.
30 sec. Cue: boards up on cue.
SCAN boards for 1/2 first.
80%+ -> reveal, then Fluency.
Less -> change all three to percentages together, re-ask.
REVEAL after boards are scanned.
SAY: Half is 50%, then 55%, then 0.6 is 60%. Tick or fix.
trap: putting 55% last because 55 is the biggest number.
Fix: turn each into a percentage, student reorders.
notes.prep: Spaced retrieval from Term 3 Week 5: comparing fractions, decimals and percentages.

slides.title: Add with the written method: 3 digits

beats: SAY: Now the written method. Line up the places and start with the ones.
ASK: Solve it with the written method.
30 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: 825
SCAN boards for the regrouped digits.
80%+ -> reveal, next one.
Less -> model the ones and the regroup together on the board, re-ask.
REVEAL after boards are scanned.
SAY: 825. Tick or fix, and check every regroup.
trap: forgetting to add a regrouped ten.
Fix: circle each carried digit, student re-adds that column.
notes.prep: Algorithm fluency: 3 digits, then 4, then 5. Whole block under 6 minutes.

slides.title: Add with the written method: 4 digits

beats: SAY: Now 4 digits. Same method, one more column.
ASK: Solve it with the written method.
45 sec. Cue: boards up on cue.
EXPECT: 6 335
SCAN boards for the regrouped digits.
80%+ -> reveal, next one.
Less -> model the ones and the regroup together on the board, re-ask.
REVEAL after boards are scanned.
SAY: 6 335. Tick or fix, and check every regroup.
trap: forgetting to add a regrouped ten.
Fix: circle each carried digit, student re-adds that column.

slides.title: Add with the written method: 5 digits

beats: SAY: Now 5 digits. Same method, one more column.
ASK: Solve it with the written method.
60 sec. Cue: boards up on cue.
EXPECT: 63 512
SCAN boards for the regrouped digits.
80%+ -> reveal, then the learning intention.
Less -> model the ones and the regroup together on the board, re-ask.
REVEAL after boards are scanned.
SAY: 63 512. Tick or fix, and check every regroup.
trap: forgetting to add a regrouped ten.
Fix: circle each carried digit, student re-adds that column.

slides.learningIntention: We are learning to measure angles with a protractor and name them by their size.
successCriteria: I can name an angle as acute, right, obtuse, straight or reflex.
I can measure an angle by reading the scale that starts at 0.
I can explain how I know my measurement makes sense.

beats: POINT to the learning intention.
SAY: This week is all about angles. Today we measure them and name them.
SAY: Read the I can lines with me. Everyone, together, on three.
SAY: We'll start with the names and build up to measuring.
Measuring with the right scale is our big goal today.
notes.prep: SC1 naming is reachable for all; SC2 reading the right scale is the core and the exit evidence; SC3 reasonableness is the stretch.

slides.title: A quarter turn is 90°
slides.prompt: Stand up. Show a quarter turn, a half turn, a full turn.

beats: POINT to the square corner.
SAY: A quarter turn makes a square corner. That's 90 degrees.
TURN together: a quarter, a half, then all the way round.
Cue: Everyone, together, on three.
ASK: A quarter turn is 90°. What is a half turn? A full turn?
15 sec. Cue: boards up on cue.
EXPECT: 180 and 360
SCAN boards for 180 and 360.
80%+ -> write the anchor on the board, move on.
Less -> turn together again counting quarters: 90, 180, 270, 360, re-ask.
trap: writing 100 for a half turn.
Fix: add two quarter turns, 90 and 90, student rewrites.
notes.prep: Launch after the LI: every student moves, then the anchor goes on the board for the whole week. Under 4 minutes.

slides.meaning: A tool for measuring angles in degrees.
slides.example: Put its centre on the corner and read the scale that starts at 0.

notes.answer: a tool for measuring angles in degrees
beats: POINT to the word. SAY: Protractor. Say it with me. Protractor.
SAY: A protractor measures angles in degrees.
Notice it has two rows of numbers going opposite ways.
ASK: Point to where the zero is on each row of numbers.
10 sec. Cue: voices off. Point... now.
EXPECT: one 0 on the right, one 0 on the left
trap: thinking the protractor has only one scale.
Fix: trace each row with a finger, student finds both zeros.
notes.prep: The word the whole week turns on. Both zeros are named here so the I Do can use them.

slides.title: Name an angle by its size

beats: POINT to right and straight.
SAY: Right is our quarter turn, 90. Straight is our half turn, 180.
POINT to acute, then obtuse.
SAY: Acute is smaller than a quarter turn.
Obtuse sits between a quarter turn and a half turn.
POINT to reflex.
SAY: Reflex is bigger than a half turn, but not a full turn.
ASK: An angle is 120°. Which name?
10 sec. Cue: boards up on cue.
EXPECT: obtuse
trap: calling any angle over 90° obtuse, even reflex ones.
Fix: check against 180 as well, student renames.
notes.stretch: Which names are exact sizes, and which are ranges? Why?
notes.help: Hold a book corner against the angle: smaller or bigger?
notes.prep: Names hang off the anchor: 90 and 180 are the boundaries. SC1.

slides.title: Measure: the arm points right
steps: Put the centre on the vertex.
Line up 0 with one arm.
Count up from that 0 to the other arm.
Check: it is acute, so under 90°.

beats: MODEL the centre on the vertex.
SAY: First I put the centre dot right on the corner.
POINT to the inner 0.
SAY: The arm points right, so I use this 0, the inner scale.
ASK: Count up in tens with me. Where does the arm cross?
10 sec. Cue: Everyone, together, on three.
EXPECT: 65
REVEAL after the choral count.
SAY: 65 degrees. Acute, so under 90 makes sense.
trap: reading 115 on the outer scale.
Fix: finger on the 0 under the arm, student re-reads.
notes.stretch: What does the other scale say, and why do the two make 180?
notes.help: Colour the scale that starts at 0 on your arm.
notes.prep: The critical feature: the scale that starts at 0 on the arm you lined up. SC2.

slides.title: Measure: the arm points left
steps: Put the centre on the vertex.
This arm points left, so use the 0 on the left.
Count up that outer scale to the other arm.
Check: it is obtuse, so between 90° and 180°.

beats: MODEL the centre on the vertex.
SAY: Same start. Centre on the corner, flat edge on the arm.
POINT to the outer 0.
SAY: This arm points left, so I use the 0 on the left.
ASK: Acute or obtuse? Show me before we count.
5 sec. Cue: voices off, fingers up: 1 acute, 2 obtuse.
EXPECT: 2 fingers
REVEAL after fingers are scanned.
SAY: 125 degrees. Obtuse, so between 90 and 180 makes sense.
trap: reading 55 on the inner scale.
Fix: ask which 0 sits on the arm, student recounts.
notes.stretch: When could both scales give sensible numbers? How do you choose?
notes.help: Say the name first: obtuse means over 90.
notes.prep: Second model uses the other scale so the rule is the 0 on your arm, not the inside numbers. SC2 and SC3.

slides.title: Which angle is obtuse?
slides.prompt: Point to A, B or C

options.misconception: calls a right angle obtuse because it looks big
calls any angle over 90° obtuse, even reflex

beats: SAY: Three angles. Check each one against a quarter turn and a half turn.
ASK: Which angle is obtuse?
10 sec. Cue: voices off. Point... now.
EXPECT: pointing to B
SCAN the room, back row first.
80%+ -> reveal, cold call one child: why not C?
Less -> hold up the name chart, test each against 90 and 180, re-ask.
REVEAL after pointing is scanned.
SAY: B. It's more than a quarter turn but less than a half turn.
trap: pointing to C.
Fix: ask if it is more than a half turn, student renames it reflex.
notes.prep: First decision point: names before measuring. Under 80% means one more pass of the chart with the turns.

slides.title: Read the protractor
slides.ask: How many degrees is this angle?
slides.pivot: finger on the 0 under the arm, count up that row in tens
slides.followUp: cold call one board: which scale did you read, and why?

items.say: 70 degrees. The arm points left, so we read the outer scale. Tick or fix.
160 degrees, not 20. It's obtuse, so it must be over 90. Tick or fix.

say: Write each measurement on your board.
trap: reading the scale that starts at 180.
Fix: name the angle first, then check the number fits.
notes.stretch: Write both readings for each angle, then say which one is the real size.
notes.help: Colour the 0 on the arm before counting.
notes.prep: Guided practice on both scales, mixing arms that point right and left. SC2.

beats: SAY: This one is just for you. Measure it on your own.
ASK: How many degrees is this angle?
20 sec. Cue: boards up on cue.
EXPECT: 48
SCAN every board, back row first.
80%+ -> reveal, then Your turn.
Less -> rebuild on the demonstration protractor: centre, 0 on the arm, count up, re-ask.
REVEAL after boards are scanned.
SAY: 48 degrees. It's acute, so under 90 makes sense. Tick or fix.
trap: writing 132.
Fix: ask whether the angle is acute, student re-reads from the 0 on the arm.
notes.prep: The hinge before independence. Students writing 132 start on the Supported Worksheet with the teacher.

slides.title: Your turn
slides.task: Name and measure each angle on your worksheet.

beats: POINT to the steps.
SAY: Read each question, solve it carefully, then check your answers.
SAY: When you finish, the early finisher option is the Extension.
Say the steps with me. Everyone, together, on three.
CIRCULATE. Check centre on vertex and the 0 on the arm first.
TIME 20 minutes. Check-in at question 12.
trap: protractor centre off the vertex.
Fix: put the dot on the corner, student measures again.
notes.stretch: Extension: clock-hand angles and angle puzzles, with worked examples.
notes.help: Supported Worksheet: angles printed with protractors, and a hint on each question.
notes.prep: Independent practice from naming, to measuring, to worded and reasoning questions. Sheet is evidence for SC2 and SC3.

slides.title: Show what you know
questions: Write the size of this angle and its name.

beats: SAY: Last one. Measure it and name it on your board.
ASK: How many degrees is this angle, and what is its name?
20 sec. Cue: boards up on cue.
EXPECT: 135, obtuse
RECORD who writes 45: the wrong scale.
They start tomorrow's first check with the teacher.
trap: writing 45.
Fix: none now, record the name.
notes.prep: Exit evidence for SC2 with the arm pointing left, the harder scale. Drives tomorrow's grouping.

slides.reflectionPrompt: Tell your partner how you choose which scale to read.

notes.answer: open - listen for the 0 on the arm
beats: SAY: Let's read our I can lines together. Everyone, together, on three.
ASK: How sure are you that you can measure with the right scale?
5 sec. Cue: Thumbs only, voices off. Show me... now.
EXPECT: thumbs up, sideways or down
RECORD each thumb down beside the exit board.
A thumb up with 45 on the board matters most.
ASK: Tell your partner how you choose which scale to read.
20 sec. Turn and tell, partner A first.
EXPECT: the one that starts at 0 on my arm
notes.prep: Self-assessment read beside the exit evidence. Tomorrow's first check comes from both. SC2.
